blocks.text: Complex numbers extend the real numbers. They were introduced to solve equations that have no solution among the real numbers. History shows that people kept enlarging their idea of a number whenever a need arose, in the spirit of the saying "Necessity is the mother of invention": first the counting numbers, then, step by step, the negative numbers, the rational numbers, the irrational numbers and so on.

The square of a positive number and the square of a negative number are both positive. So no real number has a negative square, and the square root of a negative number does not exist among the real numbers. For centuries, square roots of negative numbers were therefore ignored. In more recent times numbers involving square roots of negative numbers have been studied in detail, and they have proved useful in many branches of pure, applied, financial and computational mathematics.

The numbers of the form \(z = a + ib\), where \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(i = \sqrt{-1}\), are called complex numbers. For example, \(3 + 4i\), \(2 - \frac{5}{7}i\) and \(-7 - 2i\) are such numbers. The set of all of them is denoted by \(C\).

blocks.latex: z = a + ib,\quad a, b \in \mathbb{R},\quad i = \sqrt{-1}
blocks.text_alt: z equals a plus i b, where a and b are real numbers and i is the square root of minus one

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) as "\(a\) and \(b\) belong to the set of real numbers". So a complex number is built from two ordinary real numbers: \(a\) stands alone and \(b\) is attached to \(i\).
In \(3 + 4i\): \(a = 3\) and \(b = 4\).
In \(2 - \frac{5}{7}i\): \(a = 2\) and \(b = -\frac{5}{7}\) (the minus sign belongs to \(b\)).
In \(-7 - 2i\): \(a = -7\) and \(b = -2\).
Why we need \(i\): the equation \(x^2 = -1\) has no real solution, because every real square is \(\ge 0\). We simply name a new number \(i\) whose square is \(-1\), i.e. \(i^2 = -1\), and build all other complex numbers from it.

blocks.title: About this unit
blocks.text:
What this unit is about: real numbers cannot answer a question as simple as "which number squared gives \(-1\)?". Unit 1 builds a bigger number system, the complex numbers \(a + ib\), in which such questions always have answers.
What you will learn: real and imaginary parts and the conjugate; adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing complex numbers; complex numbers as ordered pairs and their field properties; the Argand diagram and the modulus; equality of complex numbers and square roots of a complex number; writing polynomials as products of linear factors and solving quadratic equations by completing the square; the cube roots and fourth roots of unity; the polar form and operations in polar form; and some real-world uses (electric circuits and a simple cryptography idea).
Why it matters: with complex numbers every quadratic equation has roots, every polynomial of degree \(n\) has exactly \(n\) roots (counted with repetition), and rotations and waves can be handled with simple algebra.
Prior knowledge you need: the real numbers and their properties; expanding brackets and identities such as \((a+b)^2\) and \((a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2\); solving simple and quadratic equations; plotting points on the coordinate plane; Pythagoras' theorem; and, for the polar form later in the unit, the basic trigonometric ratios.
Where it is used: electrical engineering (alternating current, voltage and impedance), signal and image processing, control systems, physics (waves, quantum mechanics), computer graphics, and in later mathematics wherever polynomial equations are solved.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A complex number has the form \(z = a + ib\) with \(a, b\) real.
2. \(i = \sqrt{-1}\), so \(i^2 = -1\).
3. The set of all complex numbers is \(C\).
4. Complex numbers were invented because real numbers have no square roots of negative numbers.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
Writing \(i = -1\). Wrong: \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) and it is \(i^2\) that equals \(-1\).
Thinking \(b\) in \(a + ib\) must be positive. In \(-7 - 2i\) the value of \(b\) is \(-2\).
